clinicalPearls: Punched-out, painless ulcers with rolled or undermined edges and a hard-crusted base, arising at sites of skin trauma exposed to hexavalent chromium, classically over the dorsa of hands, fingers, forearms and around the nail folds.
The nasal septum is the other characteristic site: chromate exposure produces septal ulceration that may progress to painless perforation, so always examine the nose in any worker with chrome ulcers.

Hexavalent chromium (chromate, dichromate) is the corrosive, ulcerogenic and sensitising species; trivalent chromium is far less toxic to skin, which is central to understanding both prevention and substitution.
Classic exposures include electroplating, chrome tanning of leather, chromate pigment and dye manufacture, welding of stainless steel, and cement/anti-corrosion work.
A pre-existing break in the skin (cut, abrasion, cuticle tear) is usually the portal; intact skin is relatively resistant, so minor wounds must be covered before chromate work.
Ulcers are indolent and slow to heal while exposure continues but typically heal with atrophic or depressed scars once contact ceases and the wound is protected.

Chrome ulceration reflects direct corrosive injury and is distinct from chromate allergic contact dermatitis, although a worker may have both; patch testing to potassium dichromate helps identify concurrent sensitisation.
Prevention hinges on barrier protection, prompt wound care, substitution to trivalent formulations where feasible, and reducing airborne and surface chromate contamination.
reference.pathophysiology: Hexavalent chromium compounds are strong oxidising agents that penetrate skin readily, particularly through breaches in the epidermal barrier. On contact with tissue they are reduced to trivalent chromium, generating reactive intermediates and free radicals that produce direct cytotoxic and corrosive coagulative necrosis of keratinocytes and dermal tissue. This yields a localised, sharply demarcated area of tissue destruction — the chrome ulcer — with a necrotic base and surrounding reactive changes. Because chromate is not appreciably painful and impairs the local inflammatory and healing response, ulcers enlarge and persist while exposure continues. The same oxidative injury on the nasal mucosa causes septal ulceration and perforation. Separately, chromium can act as a hapten binding tissue proteins to drive a delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity, but the ulcer itself is a toxic-corrosive rather than immunological lesion.
additionalDifferentials: squamous cell carcinoma or other ulcerated neoplasm
atypical mycobacterial or deep fungal ulcer
additionalInvestigations: detailed occupational and exposure history with workplace hygiene assessment
clinical examination of hands, forearms and nasal septum for coexisting lesions
patch testing to potassium dichromate to detect concurrent chromium sensitisation
swab of the ulcer base for microbiology to exclude secondary or primary infection
skin biopsy if the ulcer is atypical, non-healing or malignancy is suspected
environmental and biological monitoring of chromium (air sampling, urinary chromium)
assessment of surface and airborne hexavalent chromium contamination in the workplace
redFlags: nasal septal ulceration or perforation indicating significant mucosal chromate exposure
non-healing or expanding ulcer with atypical margins raising concern for malignancy
clinical signs of secondary infection such as spreading cellulitis or systemic upset
multiple or recurrent ulcers signalling ongoing uncontrolled workplace exposure
features suggesting systemic chromate toxicity or coexisting respiratory disease
reference.prognosis: Individual ulcers usually heal with atrophic or depressed scarring once chromate contact ceases and the wound is protected, though healing is slow. Continued exposure leads to recurrent, persistent lesions and risks nasal septal perforation, so the outlook depends on effective exposure control.
pitfalls: Mistaking a painless chrome ulcer for a trivial wound and allowing exposure to continue.
Failing to examine the nasal septum and missing early ulceration or perforation.
Confusing the corrosive ulcer with chromate allergic dermatitis and omitting patch testing when both may coexist.
Attributing a non-healing ulcer solely to chromium and overlooking malignant transformation or infection.
Neglecting workplace hygiene and colleagues, so that source control and case-finding are incomplete.
